page.title: Holy, Holy, Holy! Lord God Almighty

revision.text:
{{Short description|Christian hymn written by Reginald Heber}} {{for|the hymn in the [[Ordinary (liturgy)|ordinary]] of the Mass|Sanctus}} {{Infobox musical composition | name = "Holy, Holy, Holy! Lord God Almighty!" | type = [[Hymn]] | image = Reginald Heber.jpg | alt = | caption = Reginald Heber | occasion = [[Trinity Sunday|Trinity]] | text = by [[Reginald Heber]] | written = | based_on = {{plainlist| * [[Sanctus]] * {{Sourcetext|source=Bible|version=King James|book=Revelation|chapter=4|verse=1|range=–11}} }} | meter = 11.12.12.10 | melody = "Nicaea" {{nowrap|by [[John Bacchus Dykes]]}} | composed = {{Start date|1861}} | published = }} "'''Holy, Holy, Holy! Lord God Almighty!'''" is a Christian [[hymn]] written by the Anglican bishop [[Reginald Heber]] (1783–1826). Written during the author's time as vicar in [[Hodnet]], Shropshire, England, the text was first published posthumously in 1826. It was set to the tune "Nicaea," by [[John Bacchus Dykes]], in the influential ''[[Hymns Ancient and Modern]].'' It remains one of Heber's most popular compositions, enduring into the 21st century in many Christian traditions. Intended for use on [[Trinity Sunday]], the text invites worshippers to join in praising the [[trinitarian]] Deity, paraphrasing {{bibleverse|Revelation|4:1–11|KJV}}. ==History== The hymn was written in the early 1800s during Heber's time as [[Vicar (Anglicanism)|vicar]] (1807–1823) in [[Hodnet]], Shropshire, England, a period in which the author was prolific, writing more than 100 hymns, many having survived to modern times.{{cite web |title=Holy, Holy, Holy! |date=5 April 2019 |url=https://www.christcovenant.church/thecovenanterblog/2019/3/10/immortal-invisible-god-only-wise-n5f7a |publisher=Christ Covenant Church}} It was first published posthumously in ''A Selection of Psalms and Hymns for the Parish Church of Banbury'' (Third Edition, 1826), and thereafter by the writer's widow in ''Hymns Written and Adapted to the Weekly Church Service of the Year'' (1827),{{cite web |title=Holy, holy, holy! Lord God Almighty |url=https://hymnology.hymnsam.co.uk/h/holy,-holy,-holy!-lord-god-almighty?q=Holy,%20holy,%20holy%20Lord%20God%20Almighty |website=The Canterbury Dictionary of Hymnology |publisher=Canterbury Press}} one of the first hymnals to group their hymns by the liturgical occasion within the church year. It was published when Anglican authorities disapproved of the singing of hymns in churches, other than [[Metrical psalter|metrical psalms]], although there was considerable informal hymn-singing in parishes.*{{cite book|last= Hughes|first= Derrick|title= Bishop Sahib: A Life of Reginald Heber|publisher= Churchman Publishing|location= [[Worthing]], UK|year= 1986 | isbn = 978-1-85093-043-3 }}, pp. 77–78 Heber originally intended to win support for their inclusion. It is popular in the Anglican tradition, having appeared in the influential ''[[Hymns Ancient and Modern]]'' (1861) as well as ''[[The English Hymnal]]'' (1906) and ''[[The New English Hymnal]]'' (1986). It is considered the author's best known and most widely used hymn, and remains popular in many denominations. It has been described as one of the rare hymns which appears "in just about every hymnal". It has been performed and recorded in various styles, by artists such as [[Steven Curtis Chapman]], [[Sufjan Stevens]], [[Hillsong United]], the [[Choir of King's College, Cambridge]], the [[Hymns (2nd Chapter of Acts album)|2nd Chapter of Acts]] and the Mormon [[Tabernacle Choir]]. ==Text== The text speaks specifically of the [[Trinity|Holy Trinity]], having been written for use on [[Trinity Sunday]], although it can also be used as a general hymn of praise throughout the [[liturgical year]]. The opening line (Holy, Holy, Holy! Lord God Almighty!) references [[Isaiah 6:3]] and [[Revelation 4:8]] and mirrors the opening line of the [[Sanctus]] (Holy, Holy, Holy, Lord God of hosts). Described as a "reverent and faithful paraphrase of Revelation 4:8–11" and of the Johannine vision of unending worship in Heaven, it is an example of Heber's dutiful attempt to avoid excessive emotionalism. A defining characteristic is that the text does not "initiate praise", but is rather an invitation to join in an endless song. Poetically, it is in the long and unusual 11.12.12.10 meter, contrasting with the shorter stanzas of most preceding English hymnody, such as that of [[Isaac Watts]] or [[Charles Wesley]]. Additionally, every single line rhymes with the initial "holy".{{cite web |last1=Nelson |first1=Stanton |title=History of Hymns: "Holy, Holy, Holy! Lord God Almighty" |url=https://www.umcdiscipleship.org/resources/history-of-hymns-holy-holy-holy-lord-god-almighty |publisher=United Methodist Church |access-date=18 May 2020}} The text has a wide scope, successively referencing humans, saints, angels and all living creatures, and its main theme is the "basic belief in the Trinity", which is shared by most denominations of the Christian church despite other differences.{{Cite web|last=Banks |first=Adelle M. |url=https://religionnews.com/2019/07/19/hymn-society-tournament-reveals-greatest-hymn-of-all-time/|title=Hymn society tournament reveals 'greatest hymn of all time'|date=2019-07-19|website=Religion News Service|language=en-US|access-date=2019-07-24}} The first stanza opens with an invitation to worship God in the morning; although variants have been sometimes used to adapt the hymn for any time of day.John Julian, Dictionary of Hymnology (1907) The second stanza magnifies the opening idea, with [[saint]]s joining "in adoring the Majesty in heaven". The third stanza describes some attributes of the Christian deity, while the final stanza is a climax of the preceding with "earth and sky and sea" joining in praising the divine. Variants to the original text in modern hymnals are relatively minor, mostly found in usage by [[Nontrinitarianism|non-trinitarian]] groups such as the [[Mormons]] {{ndash}} where the final line is changed to "God in His glory, blessed Deity!" {{ndash}} or as a push for more gender inclusive language.
Holy, Holy, Holy! Lord God Almighty! Early in the morning our song shall rise to Thee; Holy, Holy, Holy! Merciful and Mighty! God in Three Persons, blessed Trinity! Holy, Holy, Holy! All the saints adore Thee, Casting down their golden crowns around the glassy sea; [[Cherub]]im and [[seraph]]im falling down before Thee, Which wert, and art, and evermore shalt be. Holy, Holy, Holy! though the darkness hide Thee, Though the eye of sinful man, thy glory may not see: Only Thou art holy, there is none beside Thee, Perfect in power in love, and purity. Holy, holy, holy! Lord God Almighty! All thy works shall praise thy name in earth, and sky, and sea; Holy, Holy, Holy! merciful and mighty, God in Three Persons, blessed Trinity!''Hymns Ancient and Modern'' (1861). London: Novello & Co. #135.
Some [[Unitarianism|Unitarian]] hymnals also employed, deliberately, the same tune for "Bring, O morn, thy music" by [[William Channing Gannett]], which has been described as a "considered response" to the Trinitarianism of the original text. It includes deliberate quotations of Heber's text, notably the repeated final line "Who wert, and art, and evermore shalt be". This text remained popular in such denominations until recently.{{cite web |last1=Watson |first1=John Richard |title=Bring, O morn, thy music |url=https://hymnology.hymnsam.co.uk/b/bring,-o-morn,-thy-music |website=The Canterbury Dictionary of Hymnology |publisher=Canterbury Press}} ==Tune== The tune for this hymn, ''Nicaea'', was composed by [[John Bacchus Dykes]] for the first edition of ''[[Hymns Ancient and Modern]]'' in 1861.{{cite book |first=Theron |last=Brown |author2=Hezekiah Butterworth |author2-link=Hezekiah Butterworth |chapter=Holy, Holy, Holy! Lord God Almighty! |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=yw80zS-vcvEC&pg=PA66 |title=The Story of the Hymns and Tunes |publisher=BiblioBazaar |year=2008 |orig-year=1906 |page=66 |isbn=978-0-554-25576-7}}{{cite book |first=Ira David |last=Sankey |author-link=Ira D. Sankey |chapter=Holy, Holy, Holy, Lord God Almighty |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=RM2EAz7VNP0C&pg=PA364 |title=My Life and the Story of the Gospel Hymns and of Sacred Songs and Solos |publisher=BiblioBazaar |year=2008 |orig-year=1907 |pages=364–365 |isbn=978-0-559-33724-6}}{{cite book |first=Kenneth W. |last=Osbeck |chapter=Holy, Holy, Holy |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=kN-FilvMftwC&pg=RA1-PA31-IA1 |title=101 hymn stories |publisher=Kregel Publications |location=[[Grand Rapids, Michigan]] |year=1982 |pages=[https://archive.org/details/101hymnstories0000osbe/page/94 94–95] |isbn=0-8254-3416-5 |oclc=7875830 |url=https://archive.org/details/101hymnstories0000osbe/page/94 }} The tune name is a tribute to the [[First Council of Nicaea]] {{ndash}} held by the [[Roman Emperor]] [[Constantine the Great|Constantine I]] in 325 {{ndash}} which formalized the doctrine of the Trinity. Rarely separated from the lyrics since then,{{cite web |title=Holy, Holy, Holy! Lord God Almighty! |url=https://hymnary.org/text/holy_holy_holy_lord_god_almighty_early |website=Hymnary.org |access-date=12 May 2020 |language=en}} it has been noted as one of the composer's finest and shares resemblances with a 16th-century [[Lutheran chorale]], "[[Wachet auf, ruft uns die Stimme]]" by [[Philipp Nicolai]]. It is a good example of Victorian hymn tune writing, with "solid harmonies and subtle chromaticism." It begins with an ascending major triad, which can be seen as symbolizing the Trinity. Few leaps and many repeated consecutive notes lend it a chant-like character. The four-part harmonisation written by Dykes is usually unchanged in hymnals, though it is frequently transposed down a tone from the initial [[E major]]. The following setting is as it appears in ''[[The New English Hymnal]]'':{{cite web |title=The New English Hymnal page 328 |url=https://hymnary.org/hymn/NEH1985/page/328 |website=hymnary.org |language=en}} << << \new Staff { \clef treble \time 4/2 \key d \major \set Staff.midiInstrument = "church organ" \omit Staff.TimeSignature \set Score.tempoHideNote = ##t \override Score.BarNumber #'transparent = ##t \relative c' << { d2 d fis fis | a1 a | b1 b2 b | a1 fis \bar"||" a2. a4 a2 a2 | d1 cis2 a | e a b2. a4 | a\breve \bar"||" d,2 d fis fis | a1 a | b2. b4 b2 b | a1 a | \bar"||" d1 a2 a | b1 fis | g2 e e2. d4 | d\breve \bar"|." } \\ { a2 a d d | cis( e) d( cis) | b( cis) d e | fis1 d | e2 e fis e | d( e) e fis | e cis d2. cis4 | cis\breve | a2 a d d | cis( e) d( cis) | b( cis) d e | fis1 d | d1 d2 d | d1 d2( c) | b b cis2. d4 | d\breve } >> } \new Lyrics \lyricmode { } \new Staff { \clef bass \key d \major \set Staff.midiInstrument = "church organ" \omit Staff.TimeSignature \relative c << { fis2 fis d d | e( g) fis( a) | g( a) b cis | d( a) a1 | a2 a a a | fis( gis) a a | cis a gis2. a4 | a1( g!) | fis2 fis d d | e( g) fis( a) | g a b cis | d( a) fis1 | fis2( g) a c | b1 a | g2 g g2. fis4 | fis\breve } \\ { d2 d b b | a1 d | g, g'2 g | d1 d | cis2 cis d cis | b1 cis2 d | e e e2. a,4 | a\breve | d2 d b b | a1 d | g,2. g4 g'2 g | d1 d | b fis2 fis | g1 d' | g,2 g a2. d4 | d\breve } >> } >> >> \layout { indent = #0 } \midi { \tempo 2 = 90 } ==References== {{Reflist}} ==External links== * {{Wikisource-inline|The Army and Navy Hymnal/Hymns/Holy, Holy, Holy, Lord God Almighty|Holy, Holy, Holy!
